column2: Right hemithorax opacification with volume loss and the mediastinum pulled right is right lung collapse; bronchoscopy for the cause (e.g. carcinoid).
PET-CT is unreliable for nodules < 8–10 mm, misses low-avidity tumours (carcinoid, AIS) and is falsely positive in inflammation.
Adenocarcinoma is the commonest lung cancer (40–50%), especially in never-smokers and women; test for EGFR, ALK, ROS1 and PD-L1.
Painful wrists/ankles with clubbing in NSCLC is hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (periostitis); NSAIDs, bisphosphonates, treat tumour.
A malignant pleural effusion is M1a, so the cancer is stage IVA regardless of T and N; treatment is systemic.
A vascular endobronchial tumour causing collapse in a young non-smoker is a bronchial carcinoid; resection has an excellent prognosis.
Beaded septal and bronchovascular thickening radiating from the hila in metastatic breast cancer is lymphangitis carcinomatosa.
Anterior mediastinal mass with cervical and axillary nodes in a young adult is lymphoma (the 4 Ts: thymoma, teratoma, thyroid, lymphoma).
A unilateral effusion with mediastinal pleural thickening after asbestos exposure is highly suspicious of mesothelioma; pleural biopsy.
Biopsy the palpable supraclavicular node (N3): it gives histology, molecular markers and the highest stage with least risk (NICE NG122).
Hoarseness right after anaesthesia with normal cord movement is intubation-related laryngeal trauma; a nerve palsy would paralyse the cord.
FDG uptake also occurs in infection and inflammation, so an avid lesion still needs tissue diagnosis.
Mesothelioma can follow brief asbestos exposure with a 30–40+ year latency; smoking does not raise its risk; cytology is often negative.
SVC obstruction is usually malignant (lung cancer, lymphoma) from mediastinal nodes compressing the SVC; stent for rapid relief.
In SVC obstruction without stridor or cerebral oedema, get tissue first; emergency radiotherapy may obscure the diagnosis.
Suspected MSCC with deficit: give high-dose dexamethasone immediately, then whole-spine MRI within 24 h and definitive treatment.
Smoking causes ~85% of lung cancer, especially squamous and small cell; asbestos multiplies its effect.
Adenocarcinoma is the commonest lung cancer in never-smokers; asbestos raises risk of all types.
Cushing's (striae, bruising) in lung cancer means ectopic ACTH from small cell carcinoma (or carcinoid).
Clubbing is the commonest extrapulmonary sign of lung cancer (up to a third); new clubbing in > 40s needs an urgent CXR.
Lung cancer causes hypercalcaemia (PTHrP, bone metastases), not hypocalcaemia; SIADH, HPOA, adrenal metastases and Horner's are recognised.
A peripheral mass with clubbing, weight loss and effusion in a smoker is non-small cell lung cancer; clubbing is uncommon in small cell.
Calcified lung metastases are characteristic of bone/cartilage sarcomas (osteo-, chondrosarcoma) and thyroid or mucinous cancers.
A central mass with fixed monophonic wheeze and hyponatraemia in a smoker suggests small cell lung cancer (SIADH).
Consolidation with a patent bronchus gives bronchial breathing, increased vocal resonance and whispering pectoriloquy.
A malignant pleural effusion (M1a, stage IV) cannot be included in a radical radiotherapy field, so radical treatment is inappropriate.
Clubbing with painful symmetrical periostitis is HPOA, usually from lung cancer; COPD does not cause clubbing, so get a chest X-ray.
Chronic cough (> 8 weeks) always needs a chest X-ray and spirometry to exclude serious disease before treating common causes.
Dense hemithorax opacity with volume loss after upper abdominal surgery is collapse from retained secretions; analgesia, physiotherapy.
Painful eyes and blurred vision on TB treatment is ethambutol optic neuritis: stop it and get urgent ophthalmology review.
Ivacaftor is a CFTR potentiator for gating mutations, classically G551D; F508del needs a corrector plus ivacaftor.
Metastatic EGFR-mutant adenocarcinoma is treated first line with an oral EGFR TKI (osimertinib preferred).
Chronic Pseudomonas in CF accelerates decline; long-term nebulised tobramycin (or colistin, aztreonam) reduces exacerbations.
Fever, eosinophilia and new infiltrates after 2 weeks of daptomycin is drug-induced eosinophilic pneumonia: stop it and give steroids.
Chronic cough, fever and bibasal infiltrates on long-term nitrofurantoin is nitrofurantoin lung; stopping the drug is diagnostic and therapeutic.
RA causes effusions, ILD, nodules, bronchiolitis obliterans and bronchiectasis; apical fibrobullous disease belongs to ankylosing spondylitis.
Haemodynamically unstable (high-risk) PE: systemic thrombolysis (alteplase) after starting heparin; embolectomy if contraindicated.
Chronic dry cough with a large hiatus hernia and kyphosis is most likely GORD; trial a PPI.
Daytime-only breathlessness after a viral illness with normal imaging and spirometry suggests dysfunctional breathing; Nijmegen questionnaire.
Sudden pleuritic pain with hypoxaemia after travel and a raised D-dimer in COPD is most likely PE; CTPA (CXR to exclude pneumothorax).
Lifelong familial clubbing without symptoms is hereditary clubbing: reassure. New clubbing needs investigation.
A mass within an old TB cavity with an air crescent is an aspergilloma (mycetoma), which causes haemoptysis.
Massive haemoptysis in CF comes from bronchial arteries: bronchial artery angiography localises and embolises the bleeding.
The common cold (acute coryza) is caused mainly by rhinoviruses; symptomatic treatment only.
Cardiac arrest from suspected massive PE: immediate thrombolysis during CPR, continuing CPR for 60–90 min.
Seasonal cough with rhinorrhoea and watery eyes every May with normal spirometry is seasonal allergic rhinitis; antihistamine and nasal steroid.
Normal sleep reduces ventilatory drive and muscle tone, so mild hypoventilation (small PaCO2 rise) is normal.
Epworth 18 in an obese man suggests significant OSA; AHI 20/h is moderate (mild 5–14, moderate 15–29, severe ≥ 30).
New respiratory muscle weakness decades after polio is post-polio syndrome, causing nocturnal then daytime hypercapnia; nocturnal NIV.
Spinal TB (Pott disease) causes angular thoracic kyphosis/kyphoscoliosis and can lead to restrictive ventilatory failure.
